title: AI scams in Georgia and South Florida: How scammers use deepfakes to steal millions

reading.body:
This is impersonation fraud built on synthetic media. Voice cloning and deepfakes were used to reproduce the identity of a trusted person, in this case an immigration attorney, so that the victim would act on a request believing it came from someone known to them. The failure sits at the point of contact, the phone call or the social media approach, rather than inside a system that an organisation deployed and could monitor.

Nothing in the interaction itself would have let a victim separate the cloned voice from the real one. Catching it depended on verification through a channel the victim already held independently of the contact, which is a check the victim has to perform rather than one the technology performs for them. The reported loss figures come from complaints, and the reporting notes that many victims never file one, so the totals describe what was reported rather than what occurred.

It is not established which AI tools were used, who operated them, or whether any of the reported losses have been adjudicated as fraud. The figures attributed to the FBI report are counts of complaints, and a complaint is not a finding.

summary:
Scammers are increasingly using artificial intelligence to commit fraud by creating deepfakes and cloning voices to impersonate trusted individuals. In Georgia and South Florida, criminals have stolen millions using these tactics, including a case where a Cobb County couple lost approximately $800,000 in a cryptocurrency scam and an immigration attorney had his voice and identity cloned to target vulnerable immigrants. According to the FBI's 2025 Internet Crime Report, Americans reported nearly $893 million in AI-enabled scam losses in the previous year, with romance and confidence scams resulting in over $19 million in reported losses nationwide.

The problem is particularly acute in Florida and Georgia, where authorities reported 350 AI-related complaints totaling nearly $39.9 million in losses and 71 complaints totaling more than $10.4 million respectively. Experts warn these numbers likely underestimate actual losses since many victims never report being defrauded. To protect themselves, consumers should establish code words to verify loved ones' identities during emergencies, verify urgent requests through known contact information, and avoid sending money based solely on phone calls.
